analysis.one_liner: Splits the labor board evenly between the parties and lets employers challenge complaints in court before hearings.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: introduced in June 2023 with no cosponsors, it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee until the Congress ended, without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restructure the National Labor Relations Board, the agency that enforces workers' rights to organize and unions, and that rules on employers' unfair labor practices. It would expand the Board from five to six members, evenly split between the two major parties, require the President to consult the opposing party's Senate leader before appointing members, and speed up timelines so that cases the Board does not decide within a year become final without Board review. It would also let any employer or person hit with a Board complaint go straight to a federal court to try to get the complaint thrown out before any hearing, and open the agency's internal legal memos to discovery by the accused party.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially those facing union organizing drives or unfair labor practice complaints, would gain the most. They could challenge a complaint in court within 30 days and have the court block it if the agency lacks 'substantial evidence' — before any administrative hearing is held. They would also benefit from internal agency memos being handed over, and from a deadlocked 3-3 partisan Board that would struggle to issue decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing union drives and complaints

how_it_helps.text: Any person subject to a General Counsel complaint could petition a federal district court within 30 days, and the court could halt all proceedings if it finds the agency lacks substantial evidence of a violation — before a hearing takes place. [S2]
The bill requires the Board's six members to be evenly divided between the two major parties and requires four members to act, making it harder for any one party's appointees to issue decisions. [S2]

If the Board does not issue a final order within one year of an administrative law judge's report, any party can move to discharge the case, making the judge's report final with no Board review — and courts would then review it 'de novo', fresh, with no deference to the agency. [S2]
Accused parties could obtain the agency's internal advice memoranda and other internal memos related to a complaint, material normally protected from disclosure. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on the Board to enforce their right to organize would bear the cost: employers would gain a new, early tool to stall or kill complaints in court, an evenly split Board would deadlock more often, and the one-year discharge rule could let contested cases end with no agency decision at all.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers relying on labor law enforcement

drawbacks.text: An evenly split partisan Board could deadlock on contested cases, leaving workers and employers alike with no decision at all. [S2]

The one-year deadline, meant to fix the Board's long case backlog, cuts the other way too: contested cases could automatically become final on the administrative law judge's report without any Board review, skipping the agency's normal appeal process. [S2]
Requiring courts to review Board orders 'de novo' would reduce the deference courts normally give the labor agency's expertise, adding litigation costs for both sides. [S2]
Forcing disclosure of internal General Counsel and Division of Advice memoranda would expose the agency's deliberative legal analysis to parties opposing complaints. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has some defensible goals — the Board does move slowly, and single-party control of its membership has been criticized from both directions. But the mechanisms chosen are heavily weighted toward employers: early court review of complaints before any hearing, de novo court review of final orders, mandatory handover of internal agency memos, and a membership structure designed to deadlock. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the delays the bill addresses could be fixed without dismantling the Board's ability to decide cases, and that the bill's net effect would be to make union-side enforcement much harder.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended. [S4]

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on June 5, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S1] [S4]
No other member cosponsored the bill. [S3]
The committee took no further action on the bill, and its action history ends with the referral. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and management-side interests are better off because the bill died: the existing enforcement framework — a Board that can decide cases on a party-line majority, no pre-hearing court challenges to complaints, and normal court deference to agency decisions — stayed in place. Workers' organizing rights were protected from the bill's changes, though neither workers nor employers gained anything on the backlog and delay problems the bill was nominally aimed at.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, since the current enforcement framework stayed

for.name: Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Republican introduced the bill and not one Democrat or additional Republican cosponsored it; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.industry: Employers (management side, especially firms facing union organizing)
industries.note: If passed, the bill would have given employers a pre-hearing court challenge to Board complaints, internal agency memos for discovery, and de novo court review of final orders — tools that shift labor disputes toward litigation employers can better afford. Its death preserved the status quo framework. [S2]

The bill would have weakened the main enforcement channel for workers' organizing rights: a pre-hearing court veto of complaints, a deadlocked evenly split Board, and cases automatically finalizing without Board review would all make union organizing harder to enforce. [S2]
